# forestmap

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/shaheedazaad/forestmap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/shaheedazaad/forestmap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![forestmap status badge](https://shaheedazaad.r-universe.dev/badges/forestmap)](https://shaheedazaad.r-universe.dev/forestmap)
<!-- badges: end -->

forestmap draws a **forest plot with a heatmap of study properties**. Each
study in your meta-analysis is shown with its effect size and 95% confidence
interval, sorted from smallest to largest. Underneath, a heatmap shows each
study's properties (population, design, country, ...), so you can see at a
glance whether studies with particular properties tend to find larger or
smaller effects.

## Installation

Install from [r-universe](https://shaheedazaad.r-universe.dev):

```r
install.packages(
  "forestmap",
  repos = c("https://shaheedazaad.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")
)
```

## Example

You need a data frame with one row per study: its effect size, its sampling
variance (or standard error, or 95% CI bounds), and one column per study
property: a factor for categories such as study design, or a number such as
sample size. `NA` means the study doesn't report that property.

```{r data}
library(forestmap)
head(forestmap_example)
```

Tell `plot_forestmap()` which columns are which. Name the properties to set
the headings shown in the plot.

```{r example, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.75, fig.alt = "Forest plot of 60 studies sorted by effect size, with a heatmap of population, outcome measure, study design, country and sample size below."}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example,
  es = "smd",
  vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country",
    "Sample size" = "n"
  ),
  continuous_range = "label",
  y_label = "SMD (95% CI)"
)
```

Blue studies have a confidence interval entirely above zero, red ones
entirely below, and grey ones include zero. In this example, every study with
a negative effect is an RCT, while the largest positive effects come mostly
from quasi-experimental studies using self-report measures.

Sample size is a number, so it gets a single row: the darker a study's tile,
the larger the study, from 43 to 593 participants.

You can change the font, colours, text size, layout and more: see the
[articles](https://shaheedazaad.github.io/forestmap/articles/).
Saving is up to you, e.g.:

```r
p <- plot_forestmap(...)
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.png", p, width = 7, height = 5.25, dpi = 300)
```
